en: The Sutra on the Sixty-two Views Spoken by the Buddha, translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian.
Thus have I heard: At one time, the Buddha was traveling through the kingdom of Kuru, accompanied by a great assembly of one thousand bhikṣus.
There were two hundred and fifty people in all.
At that time, the heterodox practitioner Subbi and his disciple, the brahmin student Brahmāyu, followed the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.
The heterodox practitioner Subhīti slandered the Buddha countless times, as well as the Dharma and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus;
his disciple, the brahmin Brahmada, praised the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus countless times.

The disciples of these teachers then began to dispute with one another, each refuting what the other had said; they would always follow the Buddha and the community of monks when receiving invitations.
At that time, the Buddha traveled from the kingdom of Kauśala to the kingdom of Śrāvastī and stayed at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the bhikṣus were assembled in the Kāliṅga Lecture Hall, where they sat together in discussion, saying:
"What should be done about this matter?
The heterodox teacher Subhadda and his disciple, the brahmin student Brahmāyu, constantly follow the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to receive invitations."
The heterodox practitioner Subhīti slandered the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus countless times;
his disciple, the brahmin student Brahmāda, praised the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of bhikṣus countless times.
The Buddha, hearing from afar as he listened intently, heard the bhikṣus discussing this matter together. He then rose and went to the lecture hall.
Once seated, the Buddha asked the bhikṣus:
"What was the subject of your discussion just now when you gathered at the Kāliṅga lecture hall?"
The bhikṣus said to the Buddha: "Just now we were gathered together discussing how the heretic Subhadda and his disciple,
the brahmin student Brahmāyu, constantly follow the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus to receive invitations."
The heterodox practitioner Subhīti slandered the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus in countless ways;
his disciple, the brahmin Brahmada, praised the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha of bhikṣus in countless ways.
The Buddha said: "Excellent, monks!"
One should always practice two things. What are these two?
First, preaching the Dharma; second, contemplation.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If anyone slanders me, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, it is good if you do not harbor anger, malice, or grief.
If anyone slanders me, the Dharma, or the Saṅgha of bhikṣus, and you become angry, sorrowful, or distressed, that will lead to your own ruin."
"Monks! If there are those who praise me, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of monks, you should neither feel joy, nor grief and anxiety, nor elation;
for where there is elation, there is decline for you."
Furthermore, if there should be anyone who slanders me, the Dharma, or the bhikṣus, you should think to yourself:
"What that person says is not a truthful statement; such a thing does not exist for the Buddha."
"Monks! If there are those who praise me, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha of monks, you should reflect and say:
'This is indeed the case.'"
"Why is this? Because those with little knowledge have only admonitions and are unable to hear much, they simply praise the Buddha.
The bhikṣus asked the Buddha:
"Who is it that possesses but little knowledge, yet, being admonished, does not disparage the Buddha who is possessed of great learning?
The Buddha said: "That person says:..."

"The Buddha does not kill living beings; he harbors no enmity and carries neither sword nor staff. He teaches others to do good and extends compassion to all, including even the most minute insects and crawling creatures.
He does not take the property of others, but desires only to practice giving, and his mind is constantly mindful of generosity. When he sees someone plundering another, he feels pity for them.
His own conduct is inherently pure, and he does not enter into the ways of sinful laws."
They cultivate the pure brahmacarya and delight in pure conduct;
they do not take pleasure in the ways of evil desire, nor do they speak falsely.
Their words are sincere, and they delight in truth without falsehood; all people in the world trust their speech, harboring no contrary thoughts, and they themselves harbor no deluded thoughts.
One does not engage in divisive speech, nor act as a messenger to incite strife among people; if there are disputes, one reconciles them so that all may be at peace.
One does not revile others, nor does one use harsh language.
What he speaks brings joy to all people; he speaks only of what is good and never utters deceptive words.
He knows the proper time and is sincere; his speech is meaningful, his conduct is in accordance with the Dharma, and his words are gentle.
He does not sit upon high, ornate, or luxurious beds, nor does he wear fragrant flowers.
They do not listen to singing or dancing;
they do not drink alcohol, nor do they wear gold, silver, or precious jewels.
They always consume the food of the Dharma at its proper time without fail.
He does not accept male or female slaves;
he does not consume raw grain, nor does he accept chickens, sheep, or pigs;
he possesses no house or residence, nor does he engage in buying or selling.
They do not use weights, measures, inches, or spans to deceive or encroach upon others;
they are all free from using blades, staves, beatings, or threats to terrify others.

"For example, there are heterodox practitioners who are greedily attached to food; by analogy with such attachments, they dwell extensively in grain, liquor, livestock, clothing, and medical supplies."
"Śramaṇa Gautama, you possess none of these.

'For example, there are followers of other paths who, having received the food offered in faith by others, constantly perform deluded deeds because of it: they move slowly when entering or leaving, they slander and are envious, and they desire only to receive honor for themselves;
the Buddha is always free from such deluded deeds.'"

“Just as other heterodox practitioners accept the food offered by the faithful from people, yet keep livestock, villages, houses, grain, trees, fruits, melons, and vegetable gardens, taking them for their own consumption;
the Buddha has distanced himself from all such things.”

“There are other practitioners of the Way who, having received food offered in faith by the laity, lie down and rise upon high, broad, and ornate couches; they spread over these couches rugs decorated with fine gold and silver paintings, as well as the fur of elephants, horses, various beasts, and flying birds;
the Buddha avoids all such things.”
“Suppose there are followers of other paths who, having received food through the faithful offerings of others, ask one another:
‘What is the situation with the king? What is the situation with the bandits?’”
What is an army? What is combat?
What is a great minister?
What are the commanderies, kingdoms, districts, and towns? What is a woman?
And what is a lecherous person?
The Buddha remained detached from all such matters—discussions of worldly affairs, or accounts of land and sea expeditions.

"There are followers of other paths who, while receiving the food offered in faith by others, practice falsehood while appearing to be truthful; their inner intentions and outer conduct do not correspond. They display the light of the Dharma merely to seek wealth and profit, constantly coveting alms bowls."
The Buddha is entirely free from such deluded views.
"There are followers of other paths who, having received the food offered in faith by others, engage in disputes and say:
'I know the Dharma and the Vinaya; you do not know the Dharma and the Vinaya. You hold wrong views; how could you possibly understand the Dharma?'"
"I possess right view," he said,
his words being contradictory from beginning to end:
"I possess right view, whereas you hold wrong views."
"You are the loser and I am the winner;
you are the evil one, you are the partisan.
When [the opponent] no longer accepted these words, [the Buddha asked], "Should you not train in conduct? Is there anyone who can guarantee it for you?"
“The Buddha is free from such fruits of the animal realm.
‘There are followers of other paths who, while receiving the food offered in faith by others, constantly engage in games of dice and gambling, yet claim:
“I have mastered the *ganjue*, *dou*, *chupulujun*, *dusi*, and *lu*.”’”
“The Buddha has abandoned all such things.

‘There are followers of other paths who, having received food offered in faith by others, bathe themselves and smear their bodies with various perfumes; they adorn themselves, look at themselves in mirrors, carry tall parasols, wear sandals and tied-up hair, and drape themselves with pearl necklaces and tassels—the Buddha has abandoned all such things.’”

“There are other practitioners of the Way who, while receiving the food offered out of faith by others, constantly engage in manifesting evil deeds: they fight with their hands and feet, striking one another with their heads and faces; they set elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep to fight, as well as men, women, and children; they set cocks, pigs, and ducks to fight.
The Buddha has distanced himself from all such perverse and evil views.”

“There are other practitioners of the Way who, while receiving the food offered out of faith by others, engage in the occupations of animals to provide for their own livelihood; they distinguish the characteristics of swords, spears, bows, and arrows; they distinguish the marks of men and women, large and small; and they distinguish the marks of elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep.
The Buddha has distanced himself from all such matters.”

“There are followers of other paths who, while receiving the food offered out of faith by others, engage in the occupations of animals to provide for their own livelihood; they act as physicians for men, women, and children, or as physicians for elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep.
The Buddha has distanced himself from all such matters.”

“There are certain heterodox practitioners who, while receiving the food offered out of faith by others, sustain themselves by engaging in the activities of animals, performing rites for spirits and ghosts, making clothing and bedding, acting as their own physicians, acting as gynecologists, and practicing malevolent incantations.”

When women come and go, they take grass and transform it into fine food, which they give to people to eat; they then falsely demand fine goods in return, or they transform coarse clothing and give it to people, claiming it can enable them to fly.
The Buddha has distanced himself from all such matters.

“There are followers of other paths who, while receiving the food offered by the faithful, sustain themselves by engaging in the work of animals or by administering medicines to people to induce vomiting;
the Buddha has distanced himself from all such matters.”

“There are other practitioners of the Way who, while receiving the food offered out of faith by others, sustain themselves through the occupations of animals; they call out to people, commanding them to go east or west, cast spells to incite mutual fighting and litigation, beat and strike others, knock people to the ground, cast spells on women to cause miscarriages, and bind spells of reed-grass to people’s arms—the Buddha has distanced himself from all such matters.”

“There are followers of other paths who, while receiving the food offered out of faith by others, sustain themselves through the occupations of animals; they carry firewood to kindle fires, cast spells over acorn shells and grape seeds to produce smoke, cast spells to cause harm to rats or kill humans, and study incantations to know the time of birth and death for people—the Buddha has distanced himself from all such matters.”

“There are certain heterodox practitioners who, while receiving the food offered out of faith by others, sustain themselves through the occupations of livestock-keepers; one among them says it will rain heavily, while another says it will rain lightly.”
One person said that grain would be abundant; another said it would not ripen.
One person said that grain would be expensive; another said it would be cheap.
One person said there would be a great epidemic; another said there would not.
One person said, "A thief shall come to destroy this country. Another said, "There shall be a great death.
One person said, "There shall be a deposed king and there shall be a newly established king. One person said, "The earth shall shake violently," while another said, "No."
One person says the moon will be eclipsed; another says the moon will not be eclipsed.
One person says the sun will be eclipsed; another says the sun will not be eclipsed.
One person says the sun travels from east to west; another says it travels from west to east.

One person says that the moon and the lunar mansions travel from east to west, while another says they travel from west to east; it is because of this that there are auspicious and inauspicious omens. Another person says that it is for this reason that the sun, the moon, and the lunar mansions travel from east to west.
One person says that for this reason the sun, moon, and stars emerge; another says that for this reason the sun, moon, and stars enter.
One person says the clouds should cover the sun; another says they should emerge from the clouds; another says the sky should be clear and cloudless.
The Buddha is entirely free from such matters.

"There are followers of other paths who receive the food offered by the faithful out of trust, yet they sustain themselves through the occupations of animals; one person says, 'This king shall go and destroy that kingdom,' while another says, 'That king shall come and destroy this kingdom'; one person says, 'This king has few chariots, horses, or livestock.'"

Interpreting dreams for others; using incantations to render people mute or cause their mouths to clench; writing on behalf of others for payment; performing calculations or accounting for others for payment; and discriminating between the quality of colors for payment.
“The Buddha has abandoned all such things. The Buddha said:
“A śramaṇa eats but one meal a day and does not eat in the evening; he eats at the proper time and avoids eating at improper times.”
Knowing when to stop and being content with robes and bowl, he takes only as much food as is necessary.
To whatever place he travels, he carries his robes and bowl with him.
Just as wherever a flying bird goes, its two wings follow its body, so it is with the bhikṣu.
Regarding robes, bedding, and food, he takes only what is sufficient from his alms bowl; wherever he goes, his robes and bowl follow him—such is the bhikṣu.
Receiving the admonitions of the worthy ones, he practices them accordingly; observing himself, he does not engage in disputes, contemplates the Path, and acts with composure and discernment.
Seeing forms, one does not form conceptualizations, nor does one see others who are fighting or changing.
Continuously remaining in tranquility and free from delusion or confusion, no disagreeable, evil, or unwholesome states can disturb his resolve; he thus guards the faculty of the eye.
This is the chapter on how a bhikṣu honors the instructions of the worthy ones.
Thus the worthy one, having brought the faculties of his sense-doors to internal tranquility, does not harbor thoughts of strife or discord, taking only sufficient food for sustenance.

One's food should be neither too much nor too little, but exactly moderate; one should always eat only once a day, neither increasing nor decreasing this amount. This is intended merely to sustain life without exerting physical strength, but simply to keep the body at ease and free from pain, so that one possesses sufficient vigor to practice meditative concentration.
If there should be bhikṣus in the future, they should, by means of this excellence, practice and uphold the precepts;

they should, by means of this excellence, take only enough food for sustenance and contemplate the Path. During the first and last watches of the night, they should practice the Path with sublime, unshakable mindfulness.
During the day, whether sitting or walking in meditation, he does not give rise to unwholesome thoughts.
During the first watch of the night, he either walks or sits.
During the middle watch of the night, he lies down on his right side with one foot resting upon the other, his mind intent on maintaining the thought of constant desire for light.
During the latter part of the night, he sat again to contemplate the Way, or walked in meditation without thinking of unwholesome dharmas.

"If I enter the districts, kingdoms, counties, or towns to beg for alms, rising early the next morning, I shall put on my robes and take up my bowl to enter the districts, kingdoms, counties, or towns for alms, always guarding my body and sense faculties, and constantly maintaining mindfulness and focused attention."

Having finished his almsround and eaten his meal, he washed his hands and feet, set aside his bowl, and entered into solitary night-seated meditation. Whether beneath a secluded tree, in the open air, among the mountain crags and rocks, or in a grass hut by a riverbank, he sat upright without looking left or right. Free from worldly delusions, he cultivated mindful conduct and refrained from evil thoughts; with a heart of loving-kindness, he felt compassion for all people and even for the smallest crawling and flying insects.

The mind also does not contemplate evil; it abandons sensual desire and abandons sloth and torpor. It constantly contemplates the swift attainment of concentration and practices the mind without thinking of sleep.

It abandons hesitation and manifold perceptions, neither speaking of evil nor forming thoughts of it. The internal mind is tranquil and settled, abandoning external doubt and leaving behind all manifold perceptions.
One practices without committing unwholesome dharmas, and the mind does not dwell upon manifold conceptualizations; one completely abandons the five hindrances and the mind of worldly afflictions.

It is like a person who takes out a loan at interest, engages in trade as they wish, and returns the principal along with the interest with a surplus remaining; having sufficient means to support themselves, that person thinks to themselves and their heart is filled with joy.
It is like a person who has long served as a slave and, having attained liberation from that servile state, moves about with freedom; he thinks to himself:
"I was formerly a slave, but now I have been liberated and am a free citizen."
That person thought to himself, and his heart was filled with joy.
It was like a man confined in a prison who, upon encountering a general amnesty, is released; that person thinks to himself, and his heart is likewise filled with joy.

For example, suppose a person suffers from a grave illness for many years and months, but then encounters a skilled physician who treats and cures them. Once they have regained their strength, they can walk about, go out and come in, and eat their meals. That person thinks to themselves:
"In the past, I was burdened by illness for many years; now I have been cured and restored, possessing strength to eat, drink, and move about."
That person thinks to himself and is likewise filled with joy.

It is like a person carrying heavy wealth who, having traversed a perilous road, reaches a safe path with his goods and livestock all secure; that person thinks to himself and is likewise filled with joy.

The bhikṣu is also like this: having departed from and abandoned the five hindrances, he is as joyful in heart as one who has repaid a debt, as one released from confinement, as one whose chronic illness has been cured, as a slave who has become a free citizen, or as one who has escaped after traversing a perilous path.
The Buddha said:
"Those with little knowledge or who have not heard much will then slander the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said:
"The Dharma I have realized is profound and subtle; regarding that which I know and have fully understood, when my worthy disciples hear it, they immediately exclaim in praise of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha asked:
"What is this profound and subtle Dharma that I have realized and fully understood?"
When the wise disciples hear this, they immediately exclaim in praise of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said:

"If there are followers of other paths who, throughout past eons, perceive past events and have studied the various matters within countless paths, knowing the affairs therein, they all remain within the eighteen views."

If there are followers of other paths who, in future eons, perceive future events, study future events, and individually comprehend the matters within countless paths, they all fall within these forty-four views.

As for those heterodox practitioners who, throughout past kalpas, perceive past events and individually comprehend the matters within countless paths—all of which fall within the eighteen views—there are heterodox practitioners who maintain the view of eternalism and proclaim to the world that there is permanence; these are included among four of these views.
The Buddha said:
"Why are those heterodox practitioners included among the four views?
Each maintains their own view and constantly proclaims it, teaching worldly people that there is permanence."

If there is a follower of another path who, having severed sensual desire, practices dhyāna, and through the attainment of samādhi corresponding to that state, is able to recollect events from twenty kalpas in the past.
That person said:
"I have a permanent relationship with the world. Why is this so? Because—"
"I know the times of formation and destruction of past kalpas, but I do not know the times of formation and destruction of future kalpas.
That person then thought:
"He knows the affairs of the past, yet neglects the affairs of the future."
This is the first view.

Second, if there is a follower of another path who has severed craving and desire, and through the meditative absorption of the *tathāgata-samādhi*, is able to recollect events of the forty eons yet to come.
The person said:
"I have a constant relationship with the world. Why is this so? Because..."
"I do not know the times of formation and destruction of past kalpas, but I know the times of formation and destruction of future kalpas.
Thus, that person abandons the matters of the past which they do not know and dwells on the matters of the future; this is the second view.

Third, if there is a non-Buddhist practitioner who has severed craving and desire, practices with vigor, and dwells in tranquility, he may, through a state of meditative concentration corresponding to his specific attainment, recollect the events of eighty eons past and future.
That person then says: "I and the world are eternal."
"Why is this? Because I know the times of formation and destruction of past and future kalpas.
That person then conceives thoughts regarding the knowledge of the past and future; this is the third view.

Fourth, if there is a member of another religious sect who is diligent, tranquil, and single-minded, who practices the severing of evil deeds, and who, through a concentration of mind such as that described above, dwells with thoughts of tranquility while his faculties remain fixed upon deluded thoughts.
That person says to the world of their own accord:
"There is permanence. Why is this so?"
"I do not know the time of the formation and destruction of past kalpas, nor do I know the time of the formation and destruction of future kalpas.
This is the fourth view.

As for those heterodox teachers who preach the doctrine of permanence and who, for the sake of worldly people, claim that there is permanence—all of them fall within these four views and cannot transcend them.

The Tathāgata knows all this; moreover, his superior and subtle knowledge surpasses even this, and for this reason he does not instruct others. Being free from instruction, he has attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The Tathāgata knows the arising, the cessation, and the extinction of the sensations experienced through contact; the Buddha perceives them with a mind that is non-appropriating and perfectly liberated.
The Buddha said:
"The Dharma I have realized is profound and deeply illuminating. If there are wise disciples who hear it, they will immediately praise the Buddha.

As for those heterodox practitioners who, throughout past kalpas, have seen past events and contemplated past events—each delighting in speaking of their knowledge of the matters within countless paths—they all remain within the eighteen views."
Who are these heterodox practitioners?
They are those who, within past kalpas, have seen past events, recollected past events, and who, across countless paths, take delight in speaking of knowing the matters therein.
If there are followers of other paths who each claim that there is permanence and speak of permanence to the people of the world, they all fall within four views.
Who are these followers of other paths?
That is to say, he speaks of permanence and asserts permanence, teaching permanence to the people of the world.
When the kalpa is destroyed and ruined, the people of the lower realms will then ascend to be reborn in the twelfth heaven, the Ābhāsvara Heaven.
When the kalpa is destroyed and decays, those devas, their merit being thin and their lives exhausted, descend one after another.
There is a Brahmā who is born in the empty space above and becomes a great sovereign there; he says of himself:
"I have created all things; I am the most honored above them, the father of all, and my understanding of meaning surpasses that of a thousand men."
The Brahmā then thought to himself,
"Where can I find someone who will come to be born here?
At the very moment he conceived this thought, another person immediately understood and was reborn above him.
At that time, that Brahmā deity gave rise to the view and said:
"I have transformed all these people.
The people, too, gave rise to the view within themselves and said: [The same].
"The Brahmā-deva has transformed all of us into his likeness. Why is this?
Because the Brahmā-deva was born first and we were born later; therefore, he has transformed us."
The first-born Brahmā was most upright, handsome, and pure, with majestic and sublime spiritual power.

As for the other devas, their merit and fortune were inferior according to the Dharma; when their lives ended, they all gradually descended to be born in the human realm. There, they practiced diligence, abandoned craving and desire, and cultivated single-mindedness. Through the samādhi of "according to its form," they recollected the places where they had previously been born.
The person said:
"The Brahmā Heaven, which was first produced above, is eternally present; it never shifts nor does it die.
The eternally present and most venerable Brahmā Heaven has manifested as our own kind, yet we are not eternal, shifting, or immortal."
"This is called teaching that permanence is not [the truth]; this is the first view.
Second, if there is another person from a different school who asserts that there is a Brahmā, and he gives rise to such a view, saying:

'Whatever dharmas there are—form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these dharmas are permanent, unchanging, and do not die; whereas the earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, and space element are impermanent and lack solidity.'"
Among those Brahmā devas, those whose merit, fortune, and blessings were meager eventually passed away and descended to be born in the human realm.
Those individuals, being diligent, free from craving and desire, and single-minded, entered the samādhi of "according to form" and recollected their former existence as Brahmā devas.
That person says:

"Those dharmas—form, sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—are eternal and solid; whereas these elements of this world—the earth element, water element, fire element, wind element, and space element—are impermanent, lacking solidity, and subject to destruction."
This is the second view. As for the third, if there is a certain heterodox teacher, what does he say?

He claims there is a heaven named Kītāpota where beings take pleasure and enjoy themselves. After such happiness, they no longer think of their bodies or being afflicted by illness upon a bed. Because that person’s merit, fortune, and blessings were thin, they eventually pass away and are reborn among humans. That person practices diligence, leaves behind craving and desire, and with a single mind, enters a state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) according to its characteristics, recollecting his former place of birth. Then that person says:
"The pleasures and joys that those gods and humans experience are permanent, unchanging, and do not end in death.
These pleasures experienced by people in this world are impermanent, lacking solidity, and subject to death."
"Those gods are eternal, while these humans are impermanent. This is the third view.

Fourth, there are those who follow heterodox paths and say: "There is a class of gods named Saṃti; they dwell together in the upper realms. When they face one another with equanimity, they give rise to anger and leave their original seats. Those among the heavenly beings whose merit and fortune are thin eventually pass away and are reborn in the human realm."

That person practices diligence, leaves behind craving and desire, and becomes single-minded; through the concentration of the *yathābhūta-samādhi*, they recollect their former births in the heavens. That person says:
"Those devas who dwell together and enjoy themselves shall always abide in steadfastness and never perish."
‘My birth in the human realm is impermanent and lacks solidity; it is subject to death and cessation.
Those heavens are permanent, whereas I, in the human realm, am impermanent.
This is the fourth view.
The Buddha said:

“As for those various heterodox practitioners, each of whom asserts that things are permanent, and each of whom preaches permanence to the people of the world—all of them fall within these four views; they cannot transcend these four views.”
The Buddha knows all this, and moreover possesses a supreme, transcendent, and exquisite knowledge; for this reason, he neither censures nor reviles, having attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The Buddha knows sensations (*vedanā*) and their subsequent pleasures; he knows the means from which they arise and the views through which they emerge. The Buddha’s mind is free from grasping and is well-liberated. Regarding the dharmas known by the Buddha—profound and deeply illuminating—I have fully understood them all.
If there are wise disciples who hear and know this, they will then praise the Tathāgata.

If there are followers of other paths who, regarding past eons, perceive past events and recollect their former conduct—each delighting in explaining and understanding those matters across incalculable paths—all such views fall within the eighteen speculative views.
What is known by those practitioners of the Way?
It refers to certain heterodox practitioners who say:
"I was born here spontaneously; I did not come to be born from another direction."
To contemplate the view that [phenomena] arise from nowhere— that there was originally no world and now there is a world—
is to remain within these two views.
What, then, is known by those of heterodox paths?
They say: "I was born here spontaneously; I did not come from another direction to be born here.
They conceive that there was no world previously, yet now there is a world. There is a heaven named "Non-conception" (asaṃjñika), where one enters into a state without thought and without feeling.
When those devas and humans give rise to thoughts and reflections, their merit, fortune, and blessings become thin and exhausted; they eventually pass away and descend to be born in the world of men.

Those people practice diligence, depart from craving and desire, and with a single-minded concentration, enter the samādhi that corresponds to their former state; yet they can no longer recollect the place from which they previously came to be born.
That person then says:
"Originally there was no world, but now a world has just come into being.
Previously I did not exist, but now I have arisen spontaneously."
This is the first view.
Second, if there is a follower of another path who is deluded in thought, that deluded person thinks:
"Originally there was no world; now, for the first time, a world has come to be."
"I did not exist originally, but now I have arisen of my own accord. Why is this so?
Because I did not exist originally and now have arisen of my own accord, this is called 'the world was originally non-existent.'"
This is the second view.

Whatever is accepted by those of other paths—namely, the thought that "I originally came from nowhere to be born," or the view of recollecting that there is no place from which one is born; or the claim that "originally there was no world, and now it has just come to exist"—all such things fall within these two views. These two views cannot be surpassed.
The Buddha knows all this, yet his knowledge surpasses it with supreme, wondrous insight.
For this reason, he neither censures nor reviles, having attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The Buddha knows the sensations experienced as pleasure, and he knows the skillful means from which they arise and by what they are perceived; the Buddha has no grasping and his mind is perfectly liberated.
The Buddha said:
"The Dharma that I know is profound and deeply illuminating; I have fully understood it all.
If there are wise disciples who hear and understand this, they will immediately praise the Buddha."

If there are followers of other paths who, regarding past eons, perceive past events and recollect their former conduct, and who—within the realm of the calculable—each delight in explaining and understanding those matters, they all fall within the eighteen views.

There are certain heterodox practitioners: one says, "What I perceive has a limit and a bottom"; another says, "What I perceive has neither limit nor bottom"; another says, "What I perceive both has a limit and a bottom and lacks a limit and a bottom"; and another says, "What I perceive neither has a limit and a bottom nor lacks a limit and a bottom. All of these fall within these four views.
What is known by those of other paths? It is this:
if there are followers of other paths who practice in such a way that they declare of themselves regarding the world, "My words are the truth; all others are foolish and false speech."
Speaking for the sake of people in the world, he asserts the infinite, making this statement:
"There is a claim that 'I and the world are finite and infinite,' and there is also a claim that 'I and the world are neither finite nor infinite.'"
This is also a false statement; one who speaks thus is uttering deception. Why is this?
Because I see that the world is finite.
This is the first view.
As for the second, if there is a follower of another path, what does he know? He says:
My practice and my vision are infinite; that is to say, I know that both the self and the world are infinite.
Those heterodox practitioners who see in this way and practice in this way claim that the self and the world are infinite. Such people declare:
"The self and the world are infinite; what I say is the truth, and all others are deluded."
He spoke contrarily:
"The self and the world are both finite and infinite; the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite.
To speak thus is deceptive speech.
Why is this? Because "I" and "the world" are limitless.
These constitute two views.
Third, as for those heterodox practitioners, what do they know?
These heterodox practitioners perceive their practice in this way:
"I know whether the self and the world are finite or infinite; what I say is the ultimate truth, while all else is foolishness and false speech."
He speaks contrarily, saying:
"The self and the world are both finite and infinite; the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite.
One who makes such a statement is speaking falsely.
Why is this? Because I hold the view that the self and the world are both finite and infinite. This is the third view.
Fourth, if there is a person among those of other paths, what is that which he knows? That person says:
"I remember thus and I see thus: I know that the self and the world are neither finite nor infinite; what I say is the absolute truth, while all else is foolish and false speech."
He spoke contrarily, saying:
"The self and the world are finite; the self and the world are infinite; the self and the world are both finite and infinite.
To speak thus is deceptive speech.
Why is this? Because I am neither finite nor infinite in relation to the world.
This is the fourth view.
The Buddha said:

“Various heterodox practitioners say that the self and the world are finite; some say they are infinite; some say they are both finite and infinite; and some say they are neither finite nor infinite. All such views fall within these four positions, and none can transcend them.”
The Buddha knows all this, and his knowledge surpasses it, reaching the most sublime and wondrous insight.
For this reason, he neither censures nor reviles, having attained the unconditioned (*asamskṛta*).
The Buddha knows the sensations experienced as pleasant, and he knows from what causes and conditions skillful means arise; he does not accept or cling to them, for the Buddha understands them well.
The Buddha said:
"The Dharma that I know is profound and deeply illuminating.
If there are wise disciples who hear and understand it, they will then praise the Buddha."

If there are followers of other paths who, regarding past eons, perceive past events and recollect their former places of birth, and who each delight in explaining those matters across incalculable paths, they are all included within these eighteen views.
Various practitioners of the Way dispute and debate with one another; their assertions differ. If someone asks about a matter, they immediately engage in contention, their words varying as they say:
"I instruct such-and-one thus; I instruct that person thus; I instruct others thus; I instruct people thus, or not thus."
"All are contained within these four views.
Why is it that those heterodox practitioners dispute one another, their assertions being so diverse?
It is because there are various heterodox practitioners who, seeing in such a way and practicing in such a way, say:"
"I neither know nor see whether there is a future world or no future world;
I do not know that there is absolutely no future world, nor do I see it.
Regarding this matter, what I do not see, do not know, and do not contemplate, I speak of as such, and not as others speak."
That person speaks to himself alone, thinking:
"What I see is the ultimate truth; all else is delusion. The Buddha said:
“Those who accept the delusions and false views of others will, upon the death of their bodies, fall into the evil realms of the hells.

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who possess extensive knowledge, are wise and eloquent in exposition, who contemplate the meaning with truth, whose words do not deviate from reality, whose fame extends far and wide, and who have abandoned other views—if such persons come to that place and inquire with calm composure, yet [the teacher] cannot provide a definitive answer;
then those heterodox practitioners, upon death, will fall into the evil realms.”
This is the first view.
As for what is known by those of other paths, the second [view]:
that is to say, those of other paths see and speak thus:
"I do not know whether there is retribution for good and evil, nor do I know whether there is no retribution for good and evil; I neither know nor see."
If one speaks thus:

"The existence of calamities and blessings resulting from good and evil constitutes my attachment; the non-existence of calamities and blessings resulting from good and evil constitutes my detachment; if I am not attached, I shall turn back and undergo [rebirth]."

If there are śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who have practiced extensively and possess great knowledge, who are wise and eloquent in their explanations, whose realization of the meaning of the truths is profound, whose speech is consistent with reality, whose fame extends far and wide, and who have abandoned all other views—if such persons come to his presence and inquire about the matter with calm composure, he will be unable to provide an answer that dispels their doubts.
Those heterodox practitioners were filled with doubt and feared that someone might come to question them; should anyone ask, they would engage in contentious debate, saying:
"For such-and-such a person, one should teach it thus; for another person, one should teach it thus."
"It must be thus, and not otherwise; it must also be thus, and not otherwise.
This is the second view.
As for the third, what is known by those other wandering mendicants?
That is to say, those followers of other paths hold such views and speak thus:
"I do not know what is good and what is evil;
what should I practice and what should I not practice?"
What are the evil paths and what are the good paths?
What constitutes treasure in this present life and what constitutes treasure in future lives?
What kind of conduct should one constantly practice to experience suffering, and what kind of conduct should one practice to experience happiness?

"If there be any śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who possess extensive knowledge and understanding in their practice, who contemplate the meaning of the truths, whose speech is consistent with reality, whose fame extends to distant lands, and who have abandoned other views—if such persons come to his presence and inquire with composure and precision:
'What is good and what is evil that one should practice?'"
What is it that one does not practice?
What are the paths of good and evil?
What constitutes the treasure of this present life and future lives that one should constantly cultivate?
"What kind of conduct leads to suffering and what leads to happiness?
When asked this, they were unable to provide an answer; fearing the miserable realms, whenever someone questioned them, they would engage in disputes, each saying different things:
"One person should be instructed thus, another should be instructed thus; one should instruct people thus, or likewise, not thus."
This is the third view.
Fourthly, as for what a certain heterodox practitioner knows:
it is that the thoughts of that heterodox practitioner are deluded; if someone asks him about a matter, he immediately engages in dispute with them, and what they say differs from one another:

"One should instruct a certain person in this way; one should instruct another person in that way; one should act thus and not otherwise; one should also act thus and not otherwise, and likewise act thus and not otherwise."
This is the fourth view.
It refers to when followers of different paths dispute with one another, each asserting their own distinct position. When someone asks about a matter, they engage in mutual contention, saying:
"One should instruct such-and-such a person in this way; one should instruct another person in that way; it should be thus and not otherwise; and it should both be thus and not thus."
Those who hold such views all remain within the four types of views and cannot transcend them; the Buddha knows them all, and his knowledge further surpasses these as an absolutely sublime wisdom.
Therefore, he neither censures nor reviles, and thus attains non-action (*asaṃskṛta*).

The Buddha knows sensations (*vedanā*) and their subsequent pleasures; through skillful means (*upāya*), he knows from what they arise. The Buddha manifests his experience and is well-versed in the mental faculty (*manas*).
The Buddha said:
"The Dharma that I know is profound and deeply illuminating; I have fully realized it all.
If there are wise disciples who hear and understand this, they will then praise the Buddha."

If there are followers of other paths who, regarding past eons, know past events and recollect their former deeds, and who each delight in explaining and interpreting those matters across incalculable paths, they all fall within these eighteen views; these eighteen views cannot be exceeded.

The Buddha’s knowledge is such as this, yet it further transcends it with supreme, exquisite wisdom; therefore, he neither censures nor reviles, for the Buddha manifests a mind free from grasping and is perfectly adept at understanding.
The Buddha said:
"The Dharma that I know is profound and deeply illuminating; I have fully realized it all.
If there are wise disciples who hear and understand this, they will then praise the Buddha."

If there are followers of other paths who, within future eons, perceive future events, contemplate future events, practice incalculable paths, and each delight in explaining those matters, they all fall within the forty-four views.
What is known by those followers of other paths?
It refers to their knowledge of future events within future kalpas; they practice incalculable paths and each delights in explaining and interpreting those matters.

If there are followers of other paths who practice conceptualization and hold views based on conceptualization, and who explain their own conceptions to people of the world— remaining within these sixteen views—
what is it that these followers of other paths know?
This refers to the perception of conduct and the perception of views, which are explained as perceptions for the world and are included among the sixteen views.
Such is the view of these heterodox practitioners; they act accordingly and hold that there is a self with form, maintaining the perception of a future life, saying:
"My [view] is the truth; all others are delusion."
This is the first view. Furthermore, if there are followers of other paths who say:
"There is a self that is formless, yet there is no future world."
He says: "I am the one who speaks with perfect sincerity;
all others are deluded. This is the second view.
If there are followers of other paths who, practicing perceptions and holding views, explain their own perceptions to people of the world, saying:
"There is both form and formlessness, and there is a self; what I say is the truth, and all else is delusion."
This is the third view.
If there are followers of other paths who say:
"There is neither form nor absence of form; this is the self. My [view] is true and sincere, while others are deluded."
This is the fourth view.
Fifthly, if there is a certain heterodox teacher who says:
"The self is finite; my [view] is the truth, and all others are delusion."
This is the fifth view.
Sixth, if there is a certain heterodox teacher who says:
"The infinite is the self; my [view] is the truth, and all others are deluded."
This is the sixth view.
Seventh, if there is a certain heterodox practitioner who says:
"Both the finite and the infinite constitute the existence of a self; my [view] is the truth, and all others are deluded."
This is the seventh view.
Eighthly, if there is a certain heterodox practitioner who says:
"The self is neither finite nor infinite; this alone is the truth, and all else is delusion."
This is the eighth view.
Ninthly, if there is a certain follower of another path who says:
"The state of a single perception is what constitutes the self; my [view] is the truth, and all others are deluded."
This is the ninth view. As for the tenth:
if there is a certain heterodox practitioner who says, "The state of having few thoughts constitutes the existence of a self; my [view] is the truth, and all others are delusion."
This is the tenth view. As for the eleventh:
if there is a follower of another path who says, "Various thoughts constitute the self; my [view] is the truth, and all others are delusion."
This is the eleventh view. As for the twelfth:
if there are followers of other paths who say, "Innumerable thoughts constitute the self; my [view] is the truth, and all others are delusion."
This is the twelfth view. As for the thirteenth:
if there are followers of other paths who say, "Only pleasure constitutes the self; my [view] is the truth, and all others are delusion."
This is the thirteenth view.
The fourteenth is that if there are followers of other paths who say:
"Suffering exists as a self; my [assertion] is the truth, and all others are delusion."
This is the fourteenth view. As for the fifteenth:
if there is a certain follower of another path who says, "Pleasure and pain exist because there is a self; my [view] is the truth, and all others are delusion."
This is the fifteenth view.
The sixteenth is that if there is a certain heterodox teacher who says:
"Neither suffering nor pleasure constitutes the existence of a self; my [view] alone is the truth, and all others are delusion."
"This is the sixteenth view.
The Buddha said:
"Those heterodox practitioners who cultivate perceptions and views, and who themselves proclaim perceptions regarding the world, all fall within these sixteen views; they cannot transcend them."
The Buddha knows all this, and his knowledge surpasses it, being utterly sublime.
Because the Buddha knows this, he neither censures nor reviles, thereby attaining the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The Buddha knows sensations (*vedanā*) and their further experiences; he knows the skillful means from which they arise. The Buddha manifests non-attachment and possesses a mind well-liberated through receptivity (*kṣānti*).
The Buddha said:
"The Dharma that I know is profound and deeply illuminating; I have fully realized it all.
If there are wise disciples who hear and understand this, they will then praise the Buddha."

If there are followers of other paths who, in future eons, perceive future events and recollect past deeds, and who each delight in explaining matters across incalculable paths, all such things are contained within the forty-four views.
Who are these heterodox practitioners?

It refers to those heterodox practitioners who practice the view of impermanence and perceive things as impermanent, and who preach impermanence to the people of the world; they all fall within the eight views.
What is the practice of those of other paths?
It is this: they practice the view of non-perception and preach non-perception to the people of the world.
These followers of other paths, seeing and practicing in this way, hold that there is form and a self, yet there is no perception; and that after death, there is no future world.
To say, "I am the one who speaks with utmost sincerity,
while all others are deluded," constitutes the first view.
Second, if there is a follower of another path, what does he know?
He practices the perception of non-perception and views non-perception; he himself preaches non-perception to the people of the world, saying:
"In the formless realm there is a self that is without perception; after death there is no future world. My words are the truth, and all others are deluded."
This is the second view. As for the third view:
if there are followers of other paths who say, "There is both form and formlessness;
there is a self that is non-percipient; there is no afterlife; my words are the truth, and all others are deluded. This is the third view.
This is the third view. As for the fourth view:

suppose there is a certain follower of another path who holds that there is neither form nor non-form, and that there is a self and a world, yet after death there is no future life; he claims, "My [view] is the truth, and all others are delusion. This is the fourth view.
This is the fourth view. As for the fifth view:
if there is a follower of another path who says, "I am finite with respect to the world; my own words are the truth, and all others are deluded."
This is the fifth view. As for the sixth view:
if there is a certain heterodox practitioner who says, "I am infinite with respect to the world; my words are the truth, and all others are deluded."
This is the sixth view. As for the seventh view:
if there are other practitioners who hold that the world is both finite and infinite, they claim, "My view alone is the truth; all others are deluded."
This is the seventh view. As for the eighth view:
if there are followers of other paths who say, "It is neither finite nor infinite; my own [view] is the truth, and all others are deluded."
"This is the eighth view.
The Buddha said:
"If there are followers of other paths who, regarding future eons, perceive future events, their various assertions of what they know are all included within these forty-four views."
What do these heterodox practitioners know?

They claim to perceive the non-conceptual and practice the non-conceptual, yet they do not perceive even the absence of conceptualization; they claim to know that both themselves and the world are without conceptualization. All such views are contained within these eight views.

The first view: Suppose there is a certain follower of another path who holds such a view and acts accordingly, asserting that there is form and there is a self, and that after death there is a future life, and that "my [view] alone is true, while all others are deluded."
This is the first view.
Suppose there is a follower of another path who says:

"There is both form and formlessness, which constitutes the self; it is neither percipient nor non-percipient, and there is a future life after death. My words are the truth, and all others are deluded."
This is the second view. As for the third view:

if there are followers of other paths who say, "There is both form and formlessness as the self, and neither-perception-nor-non-perception in the afterlife; my words are the truth, and all others are deluded."
This is the third view. As for the fourth view:

if there are certain heterodox practitioners who maintain that there is a self which is neither material nor immaterial in the afterlife, and neither percipient nor non-percipient, asserting, "My [view] alone is true, and all others are deluded."
This is the fourth view.
As for the fifth view, if there is a certain heterodox practitioner who says:
"The self is finite; furthermore, in future lives it is neither percipient nor non-percipient. My words are the truth, and all others are deluded."
This is the fifth view. As for the sixth view:
if there is a certain teacher of another path who says, "The self is infinite;
it neither possesses perception nor lacks perception in the afterlife; my [view] is the truth, and all others are deluded."
This is the sixth view. As for the seventh view:

if there is a certain teacher of another path who says, "The self is both finite and infinite; it neither possesses perception nor lacks perception in the afterlife; my [view] is the truth, and all others are deluded."
This is the seventh view. As for the eighth view, if there is a certain teacher of another path who says:
"The self is neither finite nor infinite; it possesses neither perception nor non-perception in the afterlife. My [view] is the truth, and all others are delusion."
"This is the eighth view.
The Buddha said:

"If there are followers of other paths who practice neither-perception-nor-non-perception, hold the view of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, or practice neither-perception nor hold the view of perception, they all remain within these eight views and cannot transcend them."
The Buddha knows all this; his knowledge further surpasses it with a most sublime understanding. For this reason, he neither censures nor reviles, having attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
The Buddha knows the sensations that arise and the pleasures they undergo; through skillful means, he knows their origin. The Buddha manifests the liberation of mind through non-attachment.
The Buddha said:
"The Dharma that I know is profound and deeply illuminating; I have fully realized it all.
If there are wise disciples who hear and understand this, they shall speak of the Buddha's merits."
The Buddha said:
"If there are followers of other paths who, in future kalpas, perceive future events, their various assertions regarding the countless paths they know will all fall within the forty-four views."
What is known by those heterodox practitioners? It is this:
if there are heterodox practitioners who say, "There is no practice and no vision; there is no person, no thought, and no empty knowledge."
"All these fall within the seven views.
As for those heterodox practitioners who say:
'There is no practice and no view; there is no person who contemplates emptiness—what is it that they know?'"

That is to say, there are certain followers of other paths who hold such views regarding the self: "The self consists of the four great elements of form, born of father and mother, nourished by food and drink, clothed in garments that are impermanent and subject to bathing; when the body dies and lies upon the ground, the joints and bones fall apart and scatter to different places; the wind blows upon the body, which is shattered and utterly destroyed; thereafter, it does not undergo birth or death again in future lives, but is thus completely extinguished."
This is the first view. As for the second view, there are again other practitioners of the way who say:
"Death is not merely this disintegration; there is further a self that transcends it."
What is that "self" which is superior?
That self consists of the gods of the form realm and the gods of the desire realm; when that self dies and perishes, it will not undergo birth and death again in future lives.
This is the second view. As for the third view:
if there is a certain heterodox practitioner who says, "When I die, I do not perish in this way; there is another self that exists beyond this one, even surpassing it."
"Since this self lacks consciousness within form, when that self dies and perishes, it will not undergo birth and death again in future lives.
This is the third view. As for the fourth view, there are other heterodox practitioners who say:
"This self does not perish or disintegrate in this way; there is yet another self that surpasses it. What is this self?

It is the self that transcends all heavens of form-perception, completely exceeds the heavens of ill-will perception, and dwells in the cognition of the manifold, immeasurable sphere of infinite space."
"If this self were to die and perish, it would not undergo birth and death again in future lives.
This is the fourth view. As for the fifth view, there are other heterodox practitioners who say:
"It would be better for me to die and perish than to have another self that surpasses this one.
What is that self? It is the self that is likened to the All-Void-Knowing Heaven (Sarvākāśajñāna-deva), known by countless names as the Consciousness-Knowing Heaven (Vijñānajñāna-deva)."
"When one practices according to what one contemplates in that heavenly realm, and does not undergo destruction or decay, one will no longer undergo birth and death in future lives.
This is the fifth view. Furthermore, the sixth view belongs to another heterodox practitioner who says:
"The self does not perish or disintegrate in this manner; there is yet another self that surpasses it. What is that self?
It is said to transcend all heavens of consciousness and cognition, no longer being attached to them, and is named the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception."
"That self of mine, being a deity, dies and perishes; in a future life, it will no longer undergo birth and death.
This is the sixth view. As for the seventh view, there is another person of other paths who says:
"The self does not perish or disintegrate in this way; there is yet another self that surpasses it.
What is this self?
It is said to transcend all the heavens of non-perception."
"Those devas are without perception, yet they possess the mental formations of perception.
When those devas, who are 'selves,' die and perish, they shall no longer undergo birth and death in future lives.
This is the seventh view.
The Buddha said:

"Whatever heterodox practitioners may speak of the view of annihilation, the absence of practice, the absence of perception, the absence of a person, or the contemplation of emptiness—all of these are contained within these seven views; they cannot transcend or go beyond these seven views."
The Buddha knows all this; his knowledge further transcends it with a most sublime wisdom. For this reason, he neither censures nor disparages them, having attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Because the Buddha knows the sensations experienced as pleasure, he knows their origin and how they manifest; the Buddha is without attachment and possesses excellent understanding.
"The dharmas known by me are profound and deeply illuminating; I have fully understood them all.
If there are wise disciples who hear and know this, they shall proclaim the virtues of the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"If there are followers of other paths who, regarding future eons, perceive the future within countless paths, their various assertions all fall within the forty-four views."
Furthermore, there are other practitioners of the Way who claim of themselves:
"Now I am presently mindful and practicing the unconditioned; now I see the unconditioned.
If someone goes to them, they then speak for that person as follows:
"Present unconditioned [phenomena]"—all such views fall within the five views.
There are followers of other paths who hold such a view and whose practice is likewise; they dwell in palatial residences for their own pleasure, indulging themselves with the five desires.
That person says:
"I have now attained the unconditioned. This is the first view.
The second view is that there are other heterodox practitioners who say:
"It is not as others claim, that there is a self which is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in the present; rather, there is something else that attains the unconditioned in the present."
What is the unconditioned in the present?
It is when a bhikṣu, having detached from sensual desires and emerged from evil and unwholesome states, dwells with a mind focused on wholesome and blissful conduct; this is the first dhyāna.
"When that person has been extinguished, I shall no longer undergo birth and death in future lives; thus, in the present, I have attained the unconditioned (*asamskrta*).
This is the second view.
Furthermore, there is a third view held by certain śramaṇas and practitioners who say:
"It is not as others have said. It is not by means of this self that one presently attains the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*); there is yet another present unconditioned that surpasses it.
What is meant by the present unconditioned? "

That bhikṣu extinguishes mental activity and attains internal tranquility; with his will unified, he neither thinks nor acts, and through the joy of samādhi, he enters the second dhyāna. That person, having extinguished all things, realizes the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) in the present.
This is the third view. As for the fourth view, there are again śramaṇas and practitioners who say:
"It is not as others claim; one does not attain the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) through this self in the present. There is yet another present unconditioned that surpasses it."
What is the unconditioned in the present?

It is when a bhikṣu, delighting in detachment from sensual lust and rejoicing in the practice of contemplation, maintains a body that is constantly tranquil and joyful like that of a noble one; as his practice of contemplation remains ever at peace, he enters the third dhyāna.
This is the fourth view.
As for the fifth view, there is another śramaṇa or practitioner who says:
"It is not as others say; one does not attain the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) by means of this present life."
Furthermore, there is the unconditioned of the present, which surpasses even that.
What is meant by the unconditioned of the present?

It is when a bhikṣu has abandoned pleasure and abandoned pain, and being free from what was previously agreeable or disagreeable, experiences neither suffering nor pleasure, constantly upholding purity, and thus practices the fourth dhyāna.
"That person attains unconditioned cessation in the present life, and will not undergo birth and death again in future lives.
This is the fifth view.
The Buddha said:

"Regarding those who are called śramaṇas or practitioners of the Way who speak of present unconditionedness (*asaṃskṛta*), who perceive present unconditionedness, and who contemplate present unconditionedness—all of them remain within these five views and cannot transcend them."
The Buddha knows all this; moreover, his knowledge surpasses that of others, being utterly sublime.
For this reason, he neither censures nor reviles, having attained the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

The Buddha knows the sensations of pleasure experienced by beings; through skillful means, he knows their origins and manifests them. The Buddha’s mind is free from attachment and he is well-versed in liberation. "The Dharma I know is profound and deeply illuminating; I have fully understood it all."
"If there are wise disciples who hear and understand this, they shall proclaim the virtues of the Buddha.
The Buddha said:
"Those heterodox practitioners, clinging to the notion of permanence and perceiving things as permanent, preach to others: [that the self and the world are eternal]."
Regarding the four views such as "The self and the world are eternal," because one does not know how they are manifested, one fails to attain the practice of vigor on the Path.

One thus comes to know these as causes and conditions of habituation and causes and conditions of non-habituation; yet, by means of these, one forms causes and conditions for success and causes and conditions for failure, failing to find their proper place.
The Buddha said:

"Those heterodox practitioners who speak of the superior and middle paths, each asserting their own views and teaching that the world is eternal, remain caught within these two extremes. Because they do not know and do not see, they fail to attain the practice of the Path and its diligence; thus, while they claim to understand the causes and conditions of habituation and non-habituation, and the causes and conditions by which things are formed, they do not grasp their true place."
The Buddha said:

“If there are followers of other paths who each maintain the view of permanence and teach others, saying, ‘I and the world are permanent,’ and who fall within these four views, they fail to attain the Way because they do not know and do not see. Whether through the cultivation of causes and conditions or the non-cultivation of causes and conditions, they are established by such causes and conditions; yet they claim that by these very causes and conditions one does not succeed, thus failing to find the correct point.”
The Buddha said:

“Those various heterodox practitioners speak of the world as finite, or as infinite, or as both finite and infinite, or as neither finite nor infinite. As for myself and the world, being caught within these four views, because we do not know, do not see, and have not attained the practice of the Path through diligence, we are only now able to understand what constitutes the causal conditions of habituation and what constitutes the causal conditions of non-habituation.”
"By means of these causes and conditions it is established; by means of these causes and conditions it is not established; its proper place cannot be found. The Buddha said:

"Those various heterodox practitioners argue with one another, each of their teachings differing. Those who remain within the four views do so because they neither know nor see; they do not practice the path or apply themselves with diligence, and thus they fail to understand what constitutes the cultivation of causes and conditions and what does not."
"It is established by these causes and conditions; it is not established by these causes and conditions; its proper locus cannot be found.
The Buddha said:
"Those various heterodox practitioners speak of perception and the practice of perception, teaching them to others as follows:"

Regarding the statement, "I have perceptions regarding the world," among these sixteen views, because one does not know and does not see, one fails to attain the practice of diligence on the Path; thus, one comes to know what constitutes the causal conditions for habituation and what constitutes the causal conditions for non-habituation.
"By means of these causes and conditions it is established; by means of these causes and conditions it is not established; its proper place cannot be found. The Buddha said:

"Those various heterodox practitioners contemplate the signless and perceive the signless; they explain to others that 'I and the world are signless. Being among those who hold the eight views, because they neither know nor see, they fail to attain the practice of the Path through diligence."
Thus one comes to know the causes and conditions of cultivation and the causes and conditions of non-cultivation;
that by which things are accomplished through these causes and conditions, and by which they are not accomplished, cannot be grasped as a fixed locus.
The Buddha said, "Those various heterodox practitioners neither conceive thoughts nor are without thought; they teach others:
'I and the world are without thought.'"
Regarding those who abide within the eight views, because they do not know and do not see, they fail to attain the practice of diligence on the Path.
Thus, they come to recognize the causes and conditions of habituation and the causes and conditions of non-habituation.
"It is formed through these causes and conditions; it is not formed through these causes and conditions; its proper place cannot be found.
The Buddha said:
"Those various heterodox practitioners speak of annihilation and destruction, and they constantly preach this to others:"
Regarding the statement, "I and the world shall perish," which falls among the seven views: because of ignorance and lack of vision, one fails to attain the path and does not practice with diligence.
Only then does one come to know what constitutes the causal conditions for habituation and what constitutes the causal conditions for non-habituation.
"It is established by these causes and conditions; it is not established by these causes and conditions; its proper place cannot be found. The Buddha said:

"Those various heterodox practitioners speak of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) in the present and perceive impermanence in the present. When they teach others that the unconditioned exists in the present, they fall within the five views. Because they neither know nor see, they fail to attain the practice of diligence on the Path."
Thus one comes to know the causal conditions of cultivation and the causal conditions of non-cultivation;
that things are accomplished through these causal conditions and not accomplished through these causal conditions—this is not to be found.
The Buddha said:
"If there are followers of other paths who, regarding past eons, perceive past events as being infinitely diverse across various paths, they fall within the eighteen views."

Those various heterodox practitioners, throughout future eons, will perceive future events; though they speak with differing assertions across countless paths, those who hold the forty-four views are all subsumed within these sixty-two views. Moving back and forth among them, dwelling therein, they are born together and act in concert within them, caught in a net of birth and death from which they cannot escape.

The Buddha said, “It is like a skilled fisherman or a fisherman’s apprentice who takes a fine-meshed net and lowers it into a small pool; having lowered it, he stands or sits nearby. That person thinks to himself:
‘The water is shallow; the fish will swim about and all come up onto the net.’”
"Often they remain within it and cannot escape. The Buddha said:

"In this way, these various heterodox practitioners, throughout past kalpas, have seen past events and recognized their former deeds; though they speak with various differences across countless paths, they fall within the eighteen views. Furthermore, if there are heterodox practitioners who, throughout future kalpas, see future events and contemplate and speak of future events; though they speak with various differences across countless paths, they fall within the forty-four views. All of them wander back and forth within these sixty-two views, dwelling therein, undergoing birth and death therein, and moving together in unison within a net from which they cannot escape."
The Buddha said,
“Bhikṣu! The Buddha’s body has severed all attachments and always abides in its own place.”
"The devas and the people shall all see [the Buddha] while he is present, but after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they will no longer be able to see him.
When the Buddha preached this sutra, the trichiliocosm shook in six ways.
At that time, the bhikṣu Nayāharu was standing before the Buddha, fanning him with a fan.
Then the venerable Nayāharu knelt on his right knee, joined his palms, and addressed the Buddha:
"Never before has there been one such as you, O God among Gods!"
This sutra is profound; it is thus profoundly illuminating, O God among Gods!
What is the name of this sutra?
How should its name be upheld?
The Buddha told Nayāharu: "When Krakucchanda Buddha—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—preached this sutra, it was called 'The Net of Dharma' (Dharmajāla);
when Kāśyapa Buddha—the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha—preached this sutra, it was called 'The Net of Vision' (Darśanajāla)."
"Now I too shall preach this sutra, titled 'The Brahma Net.
Thus spoke the Buddha.
All the bhikṣus were filled with joy; they came forward, prostrated before the Buddha, and departed.
The Sutra on the Sixty-two Views Spoken by the Buddha, the Brahmajāla Sūtra.
